objections.original: ut ne quid posterius praeter conclusionem inferatur
objections.english: that nothing further is brought in after the conclusion
objections.objection: Praeter means 'except': after the announced divisions have been treated, nothing further should be introduced except the conclusion.
objections.why: praeter means except

objections.original: hac coniectura censentes virgines carnes edendas
objections.english: concluding from this that virgins should eat meat
objections.objection: Virgines modifies carnes, and edendas is passive: they conclude 'that virgin flesh should be eaten,' not that virgins should eat meat.
objections.why: the accusative needs virgines to go with carnes; virgins eating would be a dative

objections.original: fabricae etiam deum fibulas et alia muliebris cultus, sicut inaures, in primordio factitasse
objections.english: the smithy of the god in the beginning made brooches and other articles of women's adornment, such as earrings
objections.objection: Deum is the subject of factitasse and fabricae depends on it: 'the god of craftsmanship initially made brooches and other women's ornaments, such as earrings.' The subject is the god, not his smithy.
objections.why: deum is the subject, the god of the forge

objections.original: kai\ kai/ria ba/lletai nh=ssos
objections.english: and islands are hurled as missiles
objections.objection: The singular island receives the blow; kairia means 'in vital parts': 'and the island is struck in its vitals,' not hurled as a missile.
objections.why: Codex's reading does not fit Seneca's comparison, but it is one island, hurled with deadly aim

objections.original: dum metus a Tarquinio et bellum graue cum Etruria positum est
objections.english: while fear of Tarquin and the heavy war with Etruria were laid aside
objections.objection: The fear and war were present, not removed: 'while the threat from Tarquin and the serious war with Etruria persisted'; the following sentence explicitly makes that fear the cause of good government.
objections.why: Sallust's dum means until; while reverses the point Augustine draws from it

objections.original: in opusculis contra Rutinum olim scripsisse me noui aduersus eum libellum
objections.english: I know I wrote long ago in my short works against Rufinus, [in] a pamphlet against him
objections.objection: Eum modifies libellum: he wrote 'against that pamphlet' in his works against Rufinus; the pamphlet is the work being opposed, not his own additional pamphlet.
objections.why: Jerome wrote against Rufinus' pamphlet

objections.original: genus quidemspeciesdistribuunt
objections.english: The genus distributes the species
objections.objection: Species is the plural subject of distribuunt and genus its object: 'the species divide the genus.'
objections.why: species is the plural subject

objections.original: Species autem singula- ' rem particularemque multitudinern ab singularitatis deducit unitatem
objections.english: the species draws out a singular and particular multitude from the unity of singularity
objections.objection: The direction is reversed: the species reduces the multitude of individuals to unity; ab is evidently corrupt for ad before unitatem.
objections.why: the contrast is with gathering; ab is corrupt for ad

objections.original: bene intelligat, et si non saltem distincte ac memoriter valeat proferre
objections.english: and if he cannot at least deliver [them] clearly and from memory, let him be able to read the epistle and the gospel well
objections.objection: Si non refers to understanding: 'let him understand them well, and if not, at least be able to recite them clearly and from memory'; reading the epistle is a separate requirement.
objections.why: si non goes with the understanding

objections.original: quam ille quidquam cæperet
objections.english: before he had grasped anything
objections.objection: Cæperet represents coeperet, 'began': 'before he had begun anything,' not before he understood anything.
objections.why: Terence Ad. 397: coeperet

objections.original: ut infantem risu nigra non terreant
objections.english: so that black things do not frighten an infant into laughter
objections.objection: The ablative cannot mean 'into laughter'; risu is evidently a misreading of visu: 'so that black things do not frighten the infant by their appearance.'
objections.why: risu is a scan error for visu

objections.original: quos iSrjnTjttxoot uocat
objections.english: which he calls *Stromateis* (Miscellanies)
objections.objection: The damaged Greek represents the title 'Exegetical [books]' (ἐξηγητικούς), not Stromateis; the translation substitutes a different title.
objections.why: the garbled letters map one for one onto exegetikous

objections.original: quos clade illa posteriores loca, oppida approbant in quibus nati morati sepulti sunt, etiam quae ccondiderunt
objections.english: whom places [and] towns later than that disaster attest [as those] in which they were born, lived, were buried, and even which they founded
objections.objection: Posteriores agrees with quos, the gods, not the towns: 'the places and towns where they were born, lived and were buried, and those they founded, prove that these gods postdate that disaster.'
objections.why: posteriores goes with quos, the gods

objections.original: quemadmodum illam Plato a corporalibus separatam haereticis commendauerit agnitionem ante mortem consecutus
objections.english: how Plato, separating it from bodily things, commended to the heretics a knowledge attained before death
objections.objection: Consecutus agrees with Plato; agnitionem is its object, whereas illam is the object of commendauerit. Render: 'how Plato, having attained knowledge before death, commended this intellectual part, separated from bodily things, to the heretics.'
objections.why: consecutus goes with Plato

objections.original: δύναται δὲ καὶ τροφὴν οἰκείαν καὶ πρώτην αὐτῷ παρεσκευακέναι τὸ τοῦ ἄῤῥενος σπέρμα
objections.english: it can also have prepared a proper and primary nourishment for the semen of the male
objections.objection: The recipient is αὐτῷ ('for it'), not τὸ τοῦ ἄῤῥενος σπέρμα. With nature as the continuing subject, render: 'it can also have prepared the male semen as suitable initial nourishment for it.'
objections.why: auto is the recipient

objections.original: διακρινόντων ἁπάντων, καὶ τὴν μὲν σπανιάκις ἁμαρτάνειν τοῦ σκοποῦ, τὴν δ’ ἐπιτυγχάνειν ὀλιγάκις
objections.english: as if everything were settled by it, and that chance rarely misses its aim and hits it seldom
objections.objection: Ἁπάντων denotes everyone who distinguishes art from chance; τὴν μὲν is art, τὴν δ’ chance. Render: 'everyone distinguishing the two: art rarely misses its aim, whereas chance seldom attains it.'
objections.why: art and chance are the two; as written it says chance rarely misses and seldom hits

objections.original: θεὸς γὰρ οὖσα ὥσπερ ἡ ἐν ἡμῖν φύσις
objections.english: For nature in us, being as it were a god
objections.objection: Nature within us is the comparison, not the subject. Render: 'For it [the power just described], being a god like nature within us.' The claim concerns the attractive power discussed in the preceding sentence.
objections.why: the English is a fair reading of the Greek

objections.original: καὶ γὰρ τὸ ἔμφυτον θερμὸν πολὺ πλείστης οὖν τροφῆς δεῖται
objections.english: for the innate heat needs very much nourishment
objections.objection: Πολὺ says that innate heat is abundant, and οὖν makes the need for food its consequence. Render: 'for the innate heat is abundant; therefore it needs a very great amount of nourishment.' The first assertion and causal link are lost.
objections.why: Aph. 1.15: the heat is abundant, and so needs food

objections.original: τοῖς δ’ ὑπὸ Θεσσάλου εἰρημένοις, ἐνταῦθα ἀπανθήσω
objections.english: here I shall pick out the things said by Thessalus
objections.objection: The dative and context indicate 'here I shall answer what Thessalus has said'; ἀπανθήσω evidently represents ἀπαντήσω, not a verb meaning 'pick out'.
objections.why: apantheso stands for apanteso, with the dative

objections.original: αἰνοδρυφὴϲ δὲ τάλαινα· τεοῦ κάτα τυμβοχόηϲα
objections.english: Wretched woman with cheeks torn in grief, having heaped up a tomb for you
objections.objection: τυμβοχόηϲα is a first-person aorist, not a participle: 'But I, a wretched woman sorely scratched in mourning, heaped up a tomb for you.'
objections.why: a first-person aorist

objections.original: καὶ ἔστιν οὐκ ἐν ἐκείνῳ ἀλλ’ ἐν τῷ ὁρῶντι
objections.english: and [the seeing] is not in that [image] but in the one who sees
objections.objection: The subject remains the reflection, and ἐκείνῳ refers to the smooth eye: 'the reflection is not in that eye but in the observer who sees it.'
objections.why: the subject is the reflection, and ekeino the eye

objections.original: ἀναλογώτερόν ἐϲτι τοῦ ἐκτείνοντοϲ τὸ α
objections.english: But the form that lengthens the a is more regular
objections.objection: The comparison is reversed: pharos with short a is more regular than the form with long a.
objections.why: genitive of comparison: reversed

objections.original: ἀντίθεϲιϲ ἐγένετο τοῦ ᾱ εἰϲ ε
objections.english: there was also a substitution of a for e
objections.objection: This reverses the change: e is substituted for a, as knaphos becomes knephallon.
objections.why: reversed

objections.original: Θαρϲόϲ δὲ ἐκαλεῖτο καὶ Θαρεῖϲ οἱ Κίλικεϲ
objections.english: The Cilicians were also called Tharsos and Thareis
objections.objection: Tharsos names the city: 'It was also called Tharsos, and the Cilicians were called Thareis.'

objections.original: ἵν’ ἀμαζόνεϲ ἄνδρεϲ ἔωϲιν
objections.english: so that there may be breastless men
objections.objection: The adjective ἀμαζών means 'without barley-bread', not 'breastless': 'so that the men may be without bread.'
objections.why: breastless men is absurd and not secure either way; leave the word

objections.original: τὸν Πόντον τὸν Εὔξεινον κατʼ ἐξοχήν τῶν ἄλλων τότε ὑπονοούμενον μέγιστον εἶναι, πρὸς ὠκεανὸν μυθολογεῖ
objections.english: He tells the myth of the Euxine Pontus as [being] next to the ocean
objections.objection: Homer represents the Euxine as Ocean in his myth; he is not placing it next to Ocean.
objections.why: Strabo: Homer turns the Euxine into Ocean

objections.original: τίς ἂν εἰς ζῶντας τελῶν τούτων ἀνάσχοιτο
objections.english: who could bear these men when they come to be counted among the living
objections.objection: The singular participle modifies 'who', not 'these men': 'Who among the living could put up with these men?' There is no temporal clause.
objections.why: the singular participle goes with who

objections.original: κληρονομεῖν τὰ σώματα τῆς τύχης
objections.english: their bodies become the inheritance of fortune
objections.objection: The bodies inherit or share the fate of the damaged things; they do not become Fortune's inheritance.
objections.why: tes tyches is the object: the bodies share the fate

objections.original: ἐξ ἑνὸς στίχου δέδεικται λαβών
objections.english: For he has shown the definition of the magnitude of pleasures, that it is the removal of everything painful, by taking it from a single line
objections.objection: δέδεικται is passive: 'he has been shown to have taken it from a single line'; the author establishes the borrowing, rather than the borrower demonstrating the doctrine.
objections.why: dedeiktai is passive

objections.original: καὶ δι᾿ αὐτὸν ἤδη καὶ τοῦ κόσμου παιδαγωγός
objections.english: and through himself now also the tutor of the world
objections.objection: διά with the accusative expresses cause or purpose, and αὐτόν refers to humankind: 'and for humankind's sake also the tutor of the world'.
objections.why: di' auton is for humankind's sake

objections.original: ζῶντας μὲν τὸν ἐκείνων βίον
objections.english: living their death
objections.objection: The supplied Greek says 'living their life': βίον means 'life', not 'death'.
objections.why: Heraclitus fr. 62 is living their death; the English restores the sense the edition's word loses

objections.original: ἢ ἀκούων μηδενὶ προσέσχε τὸν νοῦν
objections.english: or, hearing them, paid no attention to anyone
objections.objection: μηδενί refers to Homer's verses: 'or heard them but paid attention to none of them', not to no person.
objections.why: none of them, the verses

objections.original: τὸν δὲ περὶ τῶν ψυχῶν
objections.english: the [war] for the souls
objections.objection: ψυχῶν means lives here: 'the contest in which lives were at stake', not a war for souls.
objections.why: lives at stake; the English is unclear rather than wrong

objections.original: τὸ κράτος τῆς μάχης
objections.english: the command of the battle
objections.objection: κράτος here is victory or supremacy in battle, not command of it: 'the victory in battle fell to Diomedes and Sthenelus'.
objections.why: kratos is victory

objections.original: ὃς καὶ δοκεῖ ἐκπίπτειν τὰ τροπικὰ σημεῖα
objections.english: this [circle] also appears to shift the solstitial points
objections.objection: The circle appears to deviate from the solstitial points; ἐκπίπτειν does not mean that it moves the points themselves.
objections.why: the circle departs from the points

objections.original: ἐβάρυναν ἀπολέσαντες τὰ ὑπ’αὐτῶν τρεφόμενα βρέφη
objections.english: they weighed them down by perishing, the babies being nursed by them
objections.objection: ἀπολέσαντες is active and governs βρέφη: 'they burdened the nurses by destroying the infants they were nursing', not by themselves perishing.
objections.why: apolesantes is active and governs brephe

objections.original: ἐγὼ μέλαιναν ἐξιονθίζω τρίχα
objections.english: I make my black hair sprout
objections.objection: ἐξιονθίζω means to pluck out by the roots: 'I pluck out black hair', not cause it to grow.
objections.why: reversed: exionthizo is to pluck out

objections.original: ὁ νόμος ἀπέδωκε τὴν κομιδὴν τῶν καταλειφθέντων τῇ μητρὶ
objections.english: the law gave my mother the recovery of what had been left
objections.objection: τῇ μητρί belongs with καταλειφθέντων: 'the law granted me recovery of what had been left to my mother'. The son, not his mother, receives control.
objections.why: the son recovers what was left to the mother; the law quoted next says so

objections.original: τὴν. Σικελικὴν ἀρύσηται δόξαν
objections.english: might draw his Sicilian fame
objections.objection: Here δόξαν is Empedocles' doctrine, explained by the following account of the elements, Strife and Love; render 'might derive his Sicilian doctrine'.
objections.why: doxa here is doctrine, as what follows shows

objections.original: λαιὴ δὲ κνήμη καὶ ἀριστερὸς ὦμος ἐπʼ αὐτοῦ Περσέως
objections.english: and above it the left shin and left shoulder of Perseus
objections.objection: The shin and shoulder lie on the circle, not above it; render 'and on it are Perseus' left shin and left shoulder'.
objections.why: ep' autou is on the circle

objections.original: τὸν ἐμὸν παρʼ ὑμῶν ἀπαιτήσουσι θάνατον
objections.english: will demand my death from you
objections.objection: They will demand redress for Aesop's death, not demand that he be killed; render 'will call you to account for my death'.
objections.why: as written he asks to be killed; they will exact it

objections.original: Θύρας δ᾿ ἐπίθεσθε βεβήλοις
objections.english: Shut the doors, you profane.
objections.objection: βεβήλοις is dative, identifying those to be excluded, not those addressed; render 'Shut the doors against the uninitiated'.
objections.why: the edition's dative; the sense survives

objections.original: εἰ δέ τις ἄσχετος εἴη καὶ ἀμιγὴς ταύτῃ
objections.english: if there should be a soul unattached and unmixed with this [body]
objections.objection: The feminine ταύτῃ refers to the previously described soul, not the neuter σῶμα; render 'if there is a soul independent of and unmixed with this soul'.
objections.why: the bracket has the wrong gender; the sense survives

objections.original: τῆς τοίνυν ἐν ἡμῖν ψυχῆς, ὡς καὶ Ἀριστοτέλει δοκεῖ, δυνάμει τῶν ὄντων ἐχούσης τὰ εἴδη
objections.english: the soul within us, as Aristotle also holds, possesses the forms of the things that exist in potentiality
objections.objection: δυνάμει modifies the soul's possession of forms, not the existence of the things; render 'the soul within us ... possesses potentially the forms of existing things'.
objections.why: dynamei goes with the possessing

objections.original: περὶ οὑ λέγοντα Ὄμηρον Πτολεμαῖος περὶ Βυθοῦ λέγων ἐμιμήσατο
objections.english: Zeus, about whom Homer speaks, and whom Ptolemy imitated when speaking about Depth
objections.objection: The object of ἐμιμήσατο is Homer, not Zeus; render 'Ptolemy, speaking about Depth, imitated Homer speaking about Zeus'.
objections.why: Ptolemy imitates Homer, not Zeus

objections.original: ὡς ἐν τῷ Ἀμαρτύρῳ Ἰσοκράτης
objections.english: as Isocrates in the Aeginetic [speech] without witnesses
objections.objection: The named speech is Amartyros ('Without Witnesses'); 'Aeginetic' is not the title given here. Render 'as Isocrates does in the Amartyros'.
objections.why: the speech named is the Amartyros, Isocrates 21; Aeginetic is a different speech

objections.original: τὰ γένη καθ’ ἕκαστον λοιπὸν ἐπιδεικνύναι, πῶς τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτὸ συνωνύμως κατηγορεῖται
objections.english: go on to show for each how [being] is predicated synonymously of the things under it
objections.objection: The subject is each genus, not being, which the passage calls homonymous; render 'show how each genus is predicated synonymously of the things under it'.
objections.why: each genus, not being, which the passage calls homonymous

objections.original: ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐ φοβηθησόμεθα, μή τις ἡμᾶς εὐλόγως μέμψηται
objections.english: and we shall not fear that anyone may reasonably blame us
objections.objection: This is a rhetorical question expecting assent: 'And shall we not fear that someone may reasonably blame us?' The declarative English reverses its force.
objections.why: a question expecting assent; as a statement it reverses the force

objections.original: cum quibusvis ac fere iniquis hominum iudiciis et censurae ingenii foretus exponunt
objections.english: since they expose themselves to all kinds of judgements from people, mostly unfair ones, and to criticism of their talent
objections.objection: ingenii foretus is a scan error for ingenii foetus, 'the offspring of their intellect': the object is their writings. Translate 'they expose their writings to people's judgments and criticism'.
objections.why: foretus is a scan error for foetus

objections.original: ὑπ’ ἐρώτων οὐκ εὐαγῶν ἀλλογενέσι πεισθεὶς γυναιξὶ
objections.english: persuaded by unholy passions for foreign women
objections.objection: The foreign women are the agents of persuasion; the passions explain his yielding: 'under the influence of unholy passions, persuaded by foreign women'.
objections.why: the women persuade; the passions are the condition

objections.original: οὑτωσὶ καὶ τοῖς ῥήμασιν λέγων
objections.english: speaking thus also of verbs
objections.objection: ῥήμασιν means 'words' here and specifies the wording of the quotation: 'saying this in these very words'; it does not add a claim about verbs.
objections.why: the words of the quotation, not verbs

objections.original: τὸν μέντοι Ἀλέξανδρον κἀνταῦθα ἀξιοῦ- μὲν ἀφερεπόνως τῶν Πλάτωνος ἀπομνημονεύειν δογμάτων
objections.english: Here too, however, we ask that Alexander recall Plato's doctrines without shirking labour.
objections.objection: ἀφερεπόνως means carelessly, not without shirking labour: 'Here too we regard Alexander as recalling Plato's doctrines carelessly.'
objections.why: apherepono's means carelessly; the point is a criticism

objections.original: ἄλη θείη γὰρ ὀπηδεῖ
objections.english: for it attends on Truth
objections.objection: Truth is the subject: 'for Truth accompanies it [the path of Persuasion]', not the object attended upon.
objections.why: attends on Truth is a standard reading of Parmenides 2.4

objections.original: τῷ ἑτέρῳ μόνον διαστήματι αἴτιος <οὐ> γίνεται τοῦ ποιῆσαι συμπέρασμα, οἷον τῷ ΒΓ
objections.english: it becomes the cause of producing a conclusion <not> for one interval only, for example BC
objections.objection: The supplied negation governs producing a conclusion: 'Only for one interval, e.g. BC, does it not produce a conclusion', not 'not for one interval only'.
objections.why: the negation governs producing a conclusion

objections.original: ἑωρακέναι λέγει
objections.english: he says [they] have seen
objections.objection: The understood subject of the infinitive is the reporting subject, Democritus: 'he says he has seen', not 'they have seen'.
objections.why: Democritus says they were seen; an index entry, and neither he nor they matters

objections.original: τοῖς τὸ κενὸν λέγουσιν· εἶναι τὸν τόπον ἢ διάστημα
objections.english: those who speak of the void thought, holding place to be an interval
objections.objection: The alternatives are two accounts of place: 'those who say that place is void or an interval.' X makes the interval theory a further assertion of those speaking of void.
objections.why: the two accounts of place

objections.original: τὴν ἐκ τῆς μονάδος ἐπιστροφήν
objections.english: the reversion to the monad
objections.objection: The monad is the source of the reversion: 'the reversion proceeding from the monad'; ἐκ does not mean 'to'.
objections.why: ek means from, and the parallel with the dyad needs it

objections.original: ταῦτα μὲν κατὰ Ἀριστοέλην ἀντικείμενα μόνον
objections.english: According to Aristotle, these are only opposites.
objections.objection: The restriction concerns the kinds admitted: 'According to Aristotle, these are the only kinds of opposites.' X says they are merely opposites, obscuring the contrast with Plato's intermediate kinds.
objections.why: monon restricts the kinds, as the contrast with Plato shows

objections.original: τὸ ψευδῶς εὑρίσκων ὑποκεῖσθαι τῷ μείζονι
objections.english: being falsely found to fall under the major
objections.objection: What is discovered is the falsity of the subsumption: 'being found to have been wrongly subsumed under the major.' The finding itself is not said to be false.
objections.why: what is found is the falsity

objections.original: ἐνδέχεται ἀγαθόν τι κτᾶσθαι διὰ τρόπου καὶ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ φαύλου
objections.english: it is possible to acquire some good by a way that is both good and bad
objections.objection: The good can be obtained by either sort of means: 'one can acquire a good by a good method or by a bad one,' not by a single method that is both.
objections.why: a good or a bad way, not one that is both

objections.original: δι’ ἧς τὸ ὀρεκτὸν ὂν ἀγαθὸν ἀποβέβηκεν
objections.english: through which the desired thing turned out to be good
objections.objection: The desired good results from the practice: 'through which the good that is desired has come about.' The clause does not say that something turned out to possess goodness.
objections.why: the sense survives

objections.original: Ἀπὸ τούτων τῶν ἀποσταλέντων κατὰ Σαρδικὴν τοῦ πράγματος τούτου ἕνεκα συνεκροτεῖτο ψῆφος
objections.english: Of those who were sent, on account of this matter a vote was taken against them at Serdica
objections.objection: The verdict was formed from/by these men sent to Sardica for this matter; the Greek does not say a vote was taken against them.
objections.why: apo gives who formed it; no vote against them

objections.original: ἐπὶ πολὺ τοῦτον κρατοῦντες
objections.english: mastering it for a long time
objections.objection: They retain or hold on to their anger for a long time; they do not master or subdue it.
objections.why: they hold on to their anger

objections.original: ὡς ὑπ’ ὀρόφου γινομένην
objections.english: as if made beneath a roof
objections.objection: The sound is produced by an orophos reed; the following sentence explicitly defines ὄροφος as a thin reed, not a roof.
objections.why: the next sentence defines orophos as a reed

objections.original: τὴν γινομένην ὑπὸ ὀρόφου
objections.english: one produced beneath a roof
objections.objection: This means a sound produced by the orophos reed, which the passage says is cut in meadows and made into children's pipes.

objections.original: τοὺς κατεχομένους
objections.english: those in possession of the place
objections.objection: The participle is passive: 'those being held' or 'those possessed'; it does not denote people who possess the place and release Orestes.
objections.why: passive: those held

objections.original: Ἀθηνᾶ εἰκάσασα Ἡρακλεῖ ἐποίησεν ἀναιρεθῆναι
objections.english: Athena, likening him [to one], caused him to be killed by Heracles
objections.objection: Athena identified him to Heracles and caused him to be killed; she did not liken him to a bee.
objections.why: she identified him, she did not liken him

objections.original: Ὁμήρου σχηματίζοντος ἀπὸ τοῦ μάρτυρος
objections.english: Homer forming [the word] from *martys*
objections.objection: The cited nominative is μάρτυρος (martyros), not μάρτυς (martys); that difference in declension is the point of the contrast with Zenodotus' μάρτυρες.
objections.why: the form is the point of the note

objections.original: τὴν Πιτάνην τεκοῦσαν ἀποστεῖλαι τὸ βρέφος τὴν Εὐάδνην
objections.english: Evadne, having given birth secretly at Pitane, sent the baby
objections.objection: Pitane is the mother and Evadne the baby: 'Pitane, having given birth secretly, sent the infant Evadne.'
objections.why: Ol. 6: Pitane is the mother and Evadne the baby

objections.original: ὃς οὑ τὰν Ἐπιμηθέος
objections.english: Who [is] the [daughter] of Epimetheus
objections.objection: οὑ is an evident misprint for οὐ, 'not'; the fragment means 'who does not ... the [daughter] of Epimetheus,' not an identification of the daughter.
objections.why: Pyth. 5: not the excuse of Epimetheus

objections.original: δεδιέναι φηϲὶ τῷ Ἀθάμαντι παραπλήϲια μέλλοντι θύεϲθαι
objections.english: he is afraid, since he is about to be sacrificed much like Athamas
objections.objection: μέλλοντι agrees with Athamas: he fears a fate like that of Athamas when Athamas was about to be sacrificed; the clause does not say the speaker is about to be sacrificed.
objections.why: the sense largely survives

objections.original: ἡ χεὶρ ἐπέχεται τοῦ πονηροῦ γραφέωϲ
objections.english: the hand is restrained from the wicked writer
objections.objection: The genitive identifies whose hand it is: 'the bad writer's hand is held back,' not a hand restrained from the writer.
objections.why: whose hand it is

objections.original: οὐκ ἐπὶ μειζόνων μόνον κεῖται παρὰ Θουκυδίδῃ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπ᾿ ἐλαττόνων
objections.english: it is used not only of greater matters but also of lesser ones
objections.objection: The distinction concerns the rank of the people issuing the request, not the importance of its subject: 'it is used not only of superiors but also of inferiors.'
objections.why: of superiors and inferiors, as the note on Thucydides' usage means

objections.original: βάλε δέ, βάλε, κηρύλοϲ εἴην
objections.english: cast, oh cast, would I were a kērylos
objections.objection: Here βάλε introduces a wish, reinforced by the optative εἴην; it is not a command to cast something: 'Would, oh would that I were a kērylos!'
objections.why: Alcman 26: a wish

objections.original: ὀζωτὰ
objections.english: smelly
objections.objection: ὀζωτά means 'branching' or 'knotty,' figuratively intricate, from ὄζος ('branch'); it does not mean 'smelly.' Render 'knotty and polished things.'
objections.why: ozotos is from ozos, a branch

objections.original: et disciplina vel demonstrationuncupatur
objections.english: and the discipline is called demonstration
objections.objection: Disciplina and demonstratio are alternative names, joined by vel: 'and it is called scientific knowledge or demonstration.' Disciplina is not the subject of nuncupatur.
objections.why: two names joined by vel

objections.original: quae per Ananiam et Saphiram in exordio Ecclesiae apostoli Petri severitate succisa est
objections.english: which at the beginning of the Church was cut down by the severity of the apostle Peter through Ananias and Sapphira
objections.objection: Ananias and Sapphira are the persons in whom this evil growth was cut down, not intermediaries in Peter's action: 'cut down in the persons of Ananias and Sapphira by the apostle Peter's severity.'
objections.why: per is literal, and in is clearer

objections.original: quem cum aliis opusculis ejus pariter sustinemus
objections.english: which we hold together with his other works
objections.objection: Sustinemus here means 'await': Bellator's exposition, along with his other works, is still awaited, not already held.
objections.why: he has only said he undertook it; sustinemus is await

objections.original: Fas mihi Graiorum sacrata resolvere jura
objections.english: It is lawful for me to dissolve the sacred rights of the Greeks
objections.objection: Jura here means sworn obligations, as the preceding discussion of juramentum shows: 'I may break the Greeks' sacred oaths'.
objections.why: Isidore's point is oaths

objections.original: cremedio jacet insulade criminibus
objections.english: [he] lies ... of the island
objections.objection: The recoverable 'jacet insula' means 'an island lies ...'; the island is the subject, not Jupiter.
objections.why: a damaged fragment
